segments.say: Let's take one last, slow walk back through the evening, the way you might remember a good day as you fall asleep. There's nothing to learn this time. Just a few quiet pictures, one after another, each one softer than the last. You can follow them, or let them drift past while you rest.

show.title: A slow walk back through the evening

segments.say: Picture the small restaurant again, but later now, long after the friends have gone. The candles have been blown out. The chairs are pushed in neatly around the long wooden table. The teapot has been washed and put away, its lid safely back where it belongs. The room is dark and still, resting until tomorrow.

Picture the row of hooks by the restaurant door, empty now. All the coats and scarves have gone home with their owners. The glass of the door is still a little damp from the rain. The street outside is quiet. Somewhere inside, the waiter has turned off the last light and locked up for the night.

Picture the bus stop on the wet street, its shelter glowing softly under the lamp. The teenagers with their phone have long since caught their bus. Nobody is waiting now. The puddles shine. The last bus of the night has gone by, its windows warm and nearly empty, and the street settles into silence.

Picture the gates of the little park, closed for the night. Behind them, the tall trees stand dark and still, a few last drops falling from their leaves. The paths are empty. The benches are wet. Everything in the park is resting, waiting quietly for the morning, when children will come back to run and chase and laugh.

A quiet residential street at night after rain, a row of houses with only a few windows lit, wet pavements shining under streetlamps, plane trees standing still. It's the street Nadia walked along on her way home, and perhaps a little like a street you know. Everyone behind those windows is settling down, as you are.

Picture the pedestrian crossing, the little light still changing from red to green and back again, with nobody there to cross. Patient. Steady. Keeping time through the night for no one. It doesn't need anyone to watch it. It just carries on, softly, the way your breath carries on without you needing to think about it.

Notice your breath once more. It's probably slower now than when we began. Each breath in is a little deeper. Each breath out is a little longer. You don't need to make it happen. It happens by itself, steady and patient, like the light at the crossing, all through the night.

Picture an empty school hall at night, with rows of chairs in the dark and a single lamp on the stage. All the solemn speeches are over. All the forbidden giggles have faded into memories. The pigeon, wherever it is, is asleep. The hall is completely quiet, resting until the next morning brings back the noise of children.

Picture the room Nadia glimpsed from the street, with its mobile of paper stars turning slowly over the cot. The baby inside is asleep now, breathing softly, a small hand curled by its face. One day soon, that baby will laugh for the first time. But not tonight. Tonight, there's only sleep, deep and warm and safe.

Let your attention come back to your own body. Notice how heavy it has become. Your head resting. Your shoulders soft. Your arms and hands loose. Your back sinking into the bed. Your legs heavy and still. Your feet warm. All of you, resting, held up completely by whatever is beneath you. Nothing to hold. Nothing to do.

Let the heaviness flow down through your hips, your thighs, your knees. Down through your calves and ankles, all the way to your feet. Nadia walked a long way tonight, through the rain and the quiet streets. Your legs may have carried you far today, too. Let them rest now. They don't need to walk anywhere else tonight.

Picture Nadia's front door, closed now, the lamp still glowing in the window beside it. Inside, everything is warm and quiet. The rain has stopped. The street is still. The house holds her safely, the way your own room holds you now. The door is shut. The night is outside. And you're inside, resting.

Let the pictures fade now, one by one. The restaurant. The bus stop. The park. The crossing. The school hall. The nursery. They're growing softer and further away, like lights seen from a train at night, drifting past and disappearing into the dark. You don't need to hold onto any of them.

If there's a gentle smile on your face, the kind that comes on its own when we feel safe, let it stay. It's the oldest kind of signal there is, older than words, older than our species. It simply says, everything is all right. And for now, here, resting in the quiet, everything is.

Picture the neighbours' window on Nadia's street, the one where she heard laughter in a language she doesn't speak. It's dark now. The phone call is over. The family are asleep, their laughter resting until tomorrow, when it will come back as easily as ever, in their own words, at their own table.

Picture the little teapot on the table beside Nadia's chair, its lid firmly in place, the last of the tea grown cold. It's the smallest, silliest object in our whole evening, and perhaps the most important. A reminder that the best moments rarely come from anything grand. They come from small, harmless accidents, shared with people we love.

Let your shoulders drop a little lower again, if they've crept up at all. Let your hands lie open and loose. Let your feet grow warm and heavy. Each part of you can rest a little more deeply than before. You've done nothing wrong and nothing needs fixing. You're simply a tired body, resting at the end of a day.

Let yourself sink a little deeper. And a little deeper still. There's no need to listen to the words any more. Let them become just a soft sound, like rain, like the hum of a quiet house. And let that sound carry you gently, slowly, all the way down into sleep.
